🐛 Describe the bug
Please provide an additional constructor for torch::lazy::Shape to accept dynamic bits (e.g. from SSA).
Currently, the only way to integrate dynamic bits into a shape class is via the following code sequence which is rather cumbersome to develop. While it's a great design choice to avoid a setter method for dynamic bits, I think we need to make it easy for shape to get dynamic bits upon creation.
Existing approach
torch::lazy::Shape shape1 = input.node->shape(0);
torch::lazy::Shape shape2 = shape1.with_symbolic_dims(shape1.is_symbolic());
return shape2;

auto type_ = input.node->shape(0).scalar_type();
auto sizes_ = input.node->shape(0).sizes();
auto is_dyn_ = input.node->shape(0).is_symbolic();
torch::lazy::Shape shape1 = torch::lazy::Shape(type_, sizes_, is_dyn_);
return shape1;

🐛 Describe the bug
@eellison has done a lot of good work fixing segfaults related to meta tensors incorrectly reporting themselves as cpu tensors (due to fake tensor) and then causing in c++ code that is subsequently expecting the tensor in question to actually be a cpu tensor and have real data. This issue is an attempt to explicate the underlying conceptual strategy for how to decide whether or not to treat a fake tensor as a cpu tensor or not.
The fundamental problem is we have two opposing requirements:

We wish fake tensors to mimic CPU/CUDA tensors as much as possible, so that a fake tensor behaves much the same way as their real brethren. This applies to both to device tests (e.g., looking at device, or is_cpu) as well as to dispatch key dispatch (relevant for any functionality keys, esp autocast)
We don't want any code that directly accesses pointer data to operate on fake tensors, as there isn't any data and you will segfault.

Here is a simple heuristic for how to distinguish:

In Python, direct data access never happens, we advertise as CPU/CUDA
In C++, where direct data access can happen, we advertise as Meta

But this is inaccurate on a number of fronts:

When we autocast, we want to get the CPU/CUDA autocast logic on meta tensors, otherwise the dtype is not accurate. But we don't set CPU/CUDA dispatch key on fake tensor, so we don't get the corresponding autocast logic. Repro:

import torch
from torch._subclasses.fake_tensor import FakeTensorMode

def f():
    x = torch.randn(2, 3, requires_grad=True)
    y = torch.randn(3, 4)
    with torch.autocast('cpu'):
        r = x @ y 
        return r 

with FakeTensorMode():
    r = f()
print(r)
# prints FakeTensor(cpu, torch.Size([2, 4]), torch.float32)
# should be bfloat32


When we query for device on a FakeTensor, this unconditionally dispatches to torch.ops.aten.device, no matter if subclass dispatch is disabled. This means that without some other logic, we will report the wrong device type in C++. This is why in_kernel_invocation_manager exists in the fake tensor implementation today

It would be good to have a clearer delineation of the boundary here. This is also intimately related to #81471 where FunctionalWrapperTensors don't have full implementation and also must avoid hitting Dense kernels.
It seems to me that the right way to do this is to focus on "direct data access". Our primary problem is avoiding direct access to data pointers. This happens only at a very specific part of the dispatch key order (Dense and similar). So we just need to make sure these keys are not runnable, either by removing the Dense from the functionality dispatch key set, or by adding another dispatch key in front of all of these keys to "block" execution of those keys (this is how Python key and wrapper subclass works).
PS What's the difference between wrapper subclass and fake tensor? At this point, it seems primarily because fake tensor "is a" meta tensor, which makes it marginally more efficient (one dynamic allocation rather than two) and means in C++ we can go straight to meta tensor implementation in the back... it's kind of weak, sorry @eellison for making you suffer with is-a haha.
cc @eellison @aorenste @bdhirsh @Chillee
Versions
master

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Currently, optimizers throw an assertion error when negative learning rates are supplied at construction. This proposal suggests removing this restriction. This issue has been raised before in #46480. However the proposed solution (#68052) which will add a maximize parameter to the constructor is not satisfactory.
Motivation
Since maximization is equivalent to minimizing the negative of a function, adding a maximize parameter to the SGD constructor does not add any new functionality but rather provides two ways of achieving the same thing, which contradicts the Python principle:

There should be one– and preferably only one –obvious way to do it.*

On the other hand, Pytorch does not provide an easy (obvious) way to train models that are defined as a solution of a min-max problem. Perhaps the most popular case is the training of Generative Adversarial Networks, where the parameters of the discriminator and generator are the equilibrium points of a min-max game. Currently, in order train GANs with Simultaneous Gradient Descent-Ascent (or variants thereof) one has to create two optimizers and write two blocks of code that are almost the same, see for example the official pytorch tutorial https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/dcgan_faces_tutorial.html
Alternatives
Instead, if we are allowed to set up a negative learning rate for some parameters, and positive learning rates for the rest of the parameters of a module, then SGD naturally becomes (Stochastic) Gradient Descent Ascent. Note that we are already allowed to set different learning rates for different parameter groups (unfortunately, they have to be both positive).
As a minimal working example consider the following:
import torch

class GAN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(
                self,
                generator: torch.nn.Module,
                discriminator: torch.nn.Module) -> None:
        self.generator = generator
        self.discriminator = discriminator

    def loss(self, real_data: torch.Tensor, noise: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.discriminator(real_data) - self.discriminator(self.generator(noise))

gan = GAN(generator=torch.nn.Linear(1, 2), discriminator=torch.nn.Linear(2, 1))

gradient_descent_ascent = torch.optim.SGD([
                {'params': gan.generator.parameters(), 'lr': 1.},
                {'params': gan.discriminator.parameters(), 'lr': -1.}
            ], lr=1.)
In this case the parameters of the generator will try to minimize the objective function (positive learning rate), while the parameters of the discriminator will try to maximize the objective function (negative learning rate). With this change, it could be possible to train such models with the same structure of the training loop that is used in simpler tasks like classification:
for real_data in train_loader:
    gradient_descent_ascent.zero_grad()
    noise = torch.randn(batch_size, 1)
    loss = gan.loss(real_data, noise)
    loss.backward()
    gradient_descent_ascent.step()
which is a much cleaner approach and would immediately provide the equivalent versions of Adam, Adagrad, etc. for min-max problems. Currently I am just copying the source code for SGD and removing the line that checks for positivity of the learning rate. Everything works as expected and the code is much cleaner when dealing with min-max problems. I cannot think of any risk in allowing negative learning rates. Throwing a warning might be enough, or adding a parameter allow_negative_lr with False as default might be more conservative (but clunky) solutions.
Additional context
No response

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
When the python function tracer starts, there are generally frames which are already live in the cPython interpreter. In order to produce a comprehensible trace we treat them as though they just started: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/csrc/autograd/profiler_python.cpp#L538 However, this will cause a problem when we support multiple python threads because all of these initial events will use the system TID of the thread which started the tracer. In order to treat them properly, we should lazily assign them system TIDs. This can be accomplished by keeping track of which events were start events (just tracking the number of start events is sufficient to reconstruct this information later) and then use the TID of the first call in the actual tracing block to assign the proper TID during post processing.
To take a concrete example:
# Initial stacks
Python thread 0: [foo()][bar()][baz()]
Python thread 1: [f0()][f1()]

Let's say we start the tracer from system thread 3. The five frames which were active when the tracer started will all be stored in the event buffer for thread 3 and in the current machinery that is the inferred TID. Suppose we see a call on Python thread 0 during profiling which occurs on system thread 2. We can use that information to change the system TID of the foo, bar, and baz frames to system TID 2 during post processing and produce a more accurate trace. (And will separate the stacks on the chrome trace.)

            t = torch.rand([4,4],dtype=datatype).to(torch.device('cuda',rank))

🐛 Describe the bug
Hi,
let me preface this by saying I'm not 100% this is PyTorch bug and it could very well be issue of type checkers.
What happens: When you're using a subclass nn.Module, which defines extra methods, according to type checkers (tested mypy and Pylance), the extra method itself gets a type Union[Tensor, Module] from __getattr__ method of nn.Module. The reason why this happens is that __getattr__ of nn.Module is defined earlier than any of the extra methods of the subclass due to MRO resolution, therefore it kicks in sooner.
This issue manifested in PyTorch Lightning when we were trying to improve typing situation there (Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning#13445). We stumbled upon this when the method register_comm_hook of torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel (which is a subclass of nn.Module) is not recognized as Callable, but as Union[Tensor, Module]
This leads to typing error: "Tensor" not callable when trying to invoke such method.
Please note, that the method can actually be invoked, but type checkers don't think so.
Simple example
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel
from typing_extensions import reveal_type

def register_hook(module: DistributedDataParallel, state: object, hook: Callable):
    reveal_type(module.register_comm_hook) # This outputs Union[Tensor, Module]
    module.register_comm_hook(state, hook) # This throws a typing error: "Tensor" not callable

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
When PyTorch is used for distributed training, DDP is normally good enough for most situations. However, when if performance of different nodes differs, the performance of the whole training will be decided by the worst node. E.g. worker 0  needs 1 second for a forward and backward pass while worker 1 needs 2 seconds, the time for one step will be 2 seconds.
So I am wondering if there is way to do semi-asynchronous training with Pytorch?
Alternatives
There is a similar library called hivemind, but it is designed for Internet while we prefer to run the training job in our cluster.
Additional context

🐛 Describe the bug
When you tag a PR with ciflow/trunk or ciflow/binaries, future commits pushed to those PRs don't cancel the older commits.
The Impact: If someone has to makes quick changes back to back and pushes multiple commits out to a trunk/binaries tagged PR within minutes of each other, each of those commits will trigger a full set of workflows even though only the most recent commit has any value
This happens because the concurrency group for those workflows includes the commit sha today, which is always unique.
Example:
concurrency:
  group: linux-binary-libtorch-cxx11-abi-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref_name }}-${{ github.ref_type == 'branch' && github.sha }}-${{ github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

Unlike normal PRs, these runs are actually triggered by the commit being given a certain tag.
Versions
This is a problem with the ci workflows, not pytorch

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Issue
The traditional SPMD full sync training requires all ranks to work together. This typically can work well with the regular gloo/nccl process group initialized in every rank.
Today some ML use cases require checkpointing/in-trainer publishing via a subset (1 or more in DDP/HSDP case) of ranks. A typical way is to create a sub process group using the dist.new_group() helper.
However, this creates challenges in various ways:

Currently the new_group() requires it to be called in all ranks (due to _store_based_barrier() call) to ensure the internal metadata (which are basically just some dicts) are consistent across all ranks. However, this means:
a. the sub pg cannot be created internally in some downstream libraries if those are then only invoked in those ranks. Sub pg creation (esp. gloo based) is useful for library authors to create more sophisticated logic for background processing.
b. it creates a potentially weird programming pattern where say if there are 2 calls in different sub groups, these groups' creation still needs to be hoisted like:

init_process_group() # world
sub_pg1 = new_group([1, 3, 5])
sub_pg2 = new_group([0])
if x:  # odd ranks
  save_checkpoint(sub_pg1)
if y:  # rank 0
  publish(sub_pg2)

It'd be more natural if it's like
init_process_group() # world
if x:  # odd ranks
  sub_pg1 = new_group([1, 3, 5])
  save_checkpoint(sub_pg1)
if y:  # rank 0
  sub_pg2 = new_group([0])
  publish(sub_pg2)

Note that this example may not be super obvious as it's simplified. In the real world a complicated trainer may have separate groups of people maintaining logic x and y.

Currently some of the calls (e.g. broadcast()) requires a src param to be passed in. This src somehow needs to be the global rank rather than the rank within the current pg. So in the case of odd ranks used, passing 0 would simply just stall the whole thing. Instead, the first rank within that group needs to be passed in which is 1. However, there's no public methods for that except the internal _get_global_rank(). Even if that's possible it's weird to use. A group local rank may be more suitable here semantically.

Proposal
The general proposal is to clarify the story around sub pg handling:

If some logic is needed in a subset of ranks, should caller pass a sub pg and invoke the call in that subset only (as opposed to invoke it in every rank and let non participating ranks return immediately)?
If a rank number is needed for certain collective calls, should the number be local to the process group?
Is a sub pg eligible to be created and destroyed in a subset of ranks (and updating metadata only in that sub group is allowed - this is currently not legit in existing API)?

This proposal would like to answer yes to all of the above.
In order to keep backward compatibility, the new_group() can be kept as is,
2 new APIs:
new_sub_group(): similar to new_group() but can be invoked in a subset of ranks.
clone(group): creates a sub process group with the same parameters as the input unless specified.
can be introduced to explicitly allow for such capability.
https://gist.github.com/xunnanxu/1cc1ea37a81d10f15339f7aca80a38bb is a hacky version of allowing sub pg to be created within a library (SPMDCounter in this case) to demonstrate the technical possibility.
In that gist:

test_do_stuff_with_sub_pg is the entry point creating 4 processes.
The body _work() uses the public api new_group() to create the 1st sub group for odd ranks.
Then the library SPMDCounter creates an internal pg, using internal methods, in the odd ranks only, for illustrative purpose for internal sync.

📚 The doc issue
In EXTENDING PYTORCH

save_for_backward() must be used when saving input or output tensors of the forward to be used later in the backward. Anything else, i.e., non-tensors and tensors that are neither input nor output should be stored directly on ctx.

It suggests that the "tensors that are neither input nor output" should be stored directly on ctx.
However in doc of save_for_backward, "tensors that are neither input nor output" are suggested to be stored by "save_for_backward"

All tensors intended to be used in the backward pass should be saved with save_for_backward (as opposed to directly on ctx) to prevent incorrect gradients and memory leaks, and enable the application of saved tensor hooks. See torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks.

And the example also show that "tensors that are neither input nor output" should be stored by "save_for_backward"
class Func(Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor, z: int):
        w = x * y * z
        out = x * y + y * z + w
        ctx.save_for_backward(x, y, w, out)
        ctx.z = z  # z is not a tensor
        return out
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_out):
        x, y, w, out = ctx.saved_tensors
        z = ctx.z
        gx = grad_out * (y + y * z)
        gy = grad_out * (x + z + x * z)
        gz = None
        return gx, gy, gz
